en: Buddhist Wisdom:
*Pramāṇamīmāṃsā* is a great legacy of the Buddhist logicians among the Indian treatises on the science of epistemology (*pramāṇa*).
Regarding its origination, expansion, and further development:
among the proponents of the *Ramaṇīya-mīmāṃsā*, in which tradition— whether Buddhist or otherwise— did this science of epistemology (*pramāṇa-śāstra*) first appear?
Due to the non-perception of extensive evidence, it is still impossible to reach a definitive conclusion regarding the Buddhist doctrines—

such as the invalidity of perception and other means of knowledge, the refutation of the three times, the defense of the theory that individuals are not real entities, the absence of selfhood, the arising of existence from non-existence, momentariness, the lack of a creator God, the absence of composite wholes, and the doctrine of consciousness-only— which were raised without external prompting in the sūtras of the *Gautamīya-pūrvapakṣa*.

Through a critical examination of the various forms concluded within those respective Buddhist Tantras, and by considering the expansion of the *pramāṇa* (epistemology) and *prema* (devotion), the thesis formulated by scholars such as Vidhubhusan Bhattacharya and Dalsukh Malvania— that the discussion of Buddhist epistemology (*bauddhapramāṇacarcā*) emerged subsequent to the *Nyāyasūtra*— is not undermined. This is evident even from the sūtras of the opposing position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

In some way, even the hypothesis that the ancient proponents of the theory of unreal cognition (*asat-vijñāna*) were the originators of the doctrines of Śūnyavāda and Vijñānavāda does not fulfill the aspiration of Nāgārjuna, Maitreya, Asaṅga, Vasubandhu, and others— who are renowned as the founders of these systems— to have their views developed subsequent to the *Nyāyasūtra*. For those doctrines found in the aforementioned sūtras, which are distinct from emptiness (*śūnya*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and non-self (*anātman*), have attained the status of established tenets within the Buddhist tantras existing therein.
They demonstrate that their own self is free from exertion and even predates the established doctrines propounded in the *Nyāyasūtra*,

and they establish this by means of refutations against the categories of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and objects of cognition (*prameya*) accepted by the Sarvāstivāda, which do not depend upon the *Nyāyasūtra*.

The validity of the doctrine of universal non-existence (sarvanāstitvavāda) held by Nāgārjuna and others, as well as the dependence of the *Sarvāstivāda* and *Mādhyamika* views upon the prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*) found in the *Nyāyasūtra*, is evident. Indeed, the discussion regarding the four means of valid cognition (*catuṣpramāṇa*), which is encountered as a prima facie position in the *Vigrahavyāvartanī* and its commentary, [is treated here].
Seeking the origin of her own emergence,
she still wanders aimlessly and without opportunity even today.
— The author of the Nyāya Sūtras.
Whatever acceptance of [a doctrine] is found within their own systems by the author of that Bhāṣya, the author of that Vārttika, and the author of its intended meaning (Tātparya),
it would be a conceptualization of something else in contradiction to that [acceptance].
Without the perception of a specific subverting means of knowledge (*bādhakapramāṇa*), no one—whether learned or not—is capable of [accepting such a view].
It is well known that the Buddhists follow logic (*tarka*), while the ancient Vedic philosophers who follow the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* oppose it. Thus, it is as follows:

It is not perceived as inconsistent that the priority of logic among Buddhists is due to their inclination toward it, while its subsequent appearance in the works of Gautama and others is due to its influence. Or rather, let there be whatever historical conjecture adorned by various theories may exist.
It is not incidental here [to discuss] this,

because by examining the Buddhist treatises on epistemology (*pramāṇa-śāstra*), one observes the relationship between what is dependent and what it depends upon among the discussions of *vāda*, *jalpa*, and *vitaṇḍā* conducted by the Buddhists alongside those of the followers of Kaṇāda and Gautama, in terms of their chronological sequence.
However, it must be elucidated by me with full clarity,
in order to examine the heterodox doctrines contained in the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* and to protect the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
Purity, through the Blessed Buddha, serves to awaken one to the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena and to bring an end to all suffering;
it is like a mother to both ethical discipline and meditative concentration, giving them birth and protecting them.
And the Great Wisdom, the Perfection of Wisdom, was placed at the forefront;
for the sake of awakening the authority of wisdom, it was proclaimed in the Hall of the Gabled Pavilion in Vaiśālī:
"Not yet, O Evil One."
"I shall attain final Nibbāna as long as my monks, having properly refuted arisen attacks from others by means of the Dhamma, teach the Dhamma accompanied by miracles" (Udāna 6.9).

The word of the Blessed One becomes even more praiseworthy. This statement from the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*—which has this very point as its core—should also be properly attended to: "O Venerable Śāriputra, the perfection of wisdom alone is that which pertains to all vehicles."
What more need be said? "Whatever is subject to arising is subject to cessation" (*yaṃ kiñci samudayadhammaṃ sabbaṃ taṃ nirodhadhammaṃ*)—(Udāna 5.3).
Without having directly known and fully mastered even a single dharma, one cannot bring about the end of suffering.
Buddha’s statements such as "I speak" (*vadāmi*) and so forth clearly illustrate a discourse that contains within it an inference based on pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Not holding in high regard the meaning established by the eternal scriptures, and proclaiming that wisdom alone is paramount— citing such statements as Nāgārjuna’s in the *Ratnāvalī* (v. 5), "Of these two,
wisdom is the primary one"— they [assert this].

Buddhist philosophers place at the forefront of the Middle Way (madhyamā pratipad), which serves as the antidote to ignorance (avidyā), the knowledge (vidyā) that culminates in direct experience and takes the form of right view (samyagdṛṣṭi).
This very field of excellence in wisdom (*prajñā*) is the ground for the festival of the Buddhist treatises on epistemology (*pramāṇa-śāstra*).
It is possible to conceive that for those followers of the Sugata who are devoted to wisdom, an addiction to epistemology arises quite naturally;
for this reason, by those proponents of the supramundane (*lokottara-vādins*), headed by Dignāga and others, [the nature of] the realization of non-dual emptiness...
Having established that the Buddha, who is the Dharmakāya itself, possesses the nature of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
and that he alone has the nature of non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*) through such statements as, "Prajñāpāramitā is non-dual gnosis; he is the Tathāgata" (*Prajñāpāramitāpiṇḍārtha*);

By means of verses such as "To him who is the embodiment of valid cognition, who seeks the welfare of the world" (Pramāṇasamuccaya 1.1), Dharmakīrti— whose subject matter is expounded in the first chapter of the *Pramāṇavārttika*— has offered salutation to that [Buddha], who is non-contradictory with respect to the Four Noble Truths.
It has been explained that the Blessed One is an authoritative person (*pramāṇabhūta*) because he is non-deceptive.
With all this in mind, it was stated by Prajñākaramati that the Blessed One is an authoritative person; thus it has been explained.
With this entire point in mind, Prajñākaragupta stated in his *Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkārabhāṣya* (p.
116) while demonstrating that "the establishment of everything proceeds from valid cognition alone":
"Because the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, taught the reality of valid cognition through both [means]."
It is eternal.
Beyond this there is nothing; therefore, the means of valid cognition and all accomplishments arise from the Tathāgata alone.
Thus,
having understood that being an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇabhūtatva*) is the defining factor for Buddhahood, the entire Buddhist system...
Whether directly or indirectly, it culminates precisely in the investigation of valid cognition (*pramāṇamīmāṃsā*). This being so,
in this short treatise, the nature of knowledge as accepted by the followers of the Sugata is measured in brief,
while that of Kaṇāda and Gautama is also addressed incidentally.
It is explained as follows:
eternal cognition, being devoid of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), lacks validity;
whereas only non-eternal cognition that is conjoined with a real entity possesses validity.
The intended view regarding the investigation of Buddhist epistemology is as follows:

the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)— namely, "that which reveals an unknown object while being non-contradictory"— is accepted by both external and internal schools of thought, and it is twofold according to the ultimate and conventional perspectives.

[The opponent's objection] is refuted. Because non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*) belongs to the realization of non-duality from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), which consists in the illumination of an object not previously known;

and because, in the case of conventional reality (*saṃvṛtisat*), both perception and inference establish validity by making known—either directly or indirectly—the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of objects not previously known through their non-contradictory nature, the validity of both [means of cognition] is established.

The well-known statement from the *Pramāṇavārttika* (2.3), beginning with "that which is capable of causal efficiency," follows the Sautrāntika doctrine of the existence of external objects as well as the Vijñānavādin doctrine of the non-dual ultimate reality of consciousness.
Furthermore, in either case, the fact that cognition possesses a correspondence with reality— which is necessary for its validity— is contradicted;
for this cognition must be biased toward the object in order to be valid.

The Buddhists first of all undertake an investigation into the nature of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), and they establish that the very principle which serves as the basis for the determination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the reality (*tattva*).

For this very reason, the position that "the establishment of the means of knowledge (māna) is dependent upon the object of knowledge (meya)," which is accepted by the proponents of external reality (vastuvādin),

becomes the established tenet (siddhānta). In the Vijñānavāda, however, although the determination of the means of knowledge is indeed understood through the object of knowledge, [it is not so in the case of the proponents of external reality].
Nevertheless, the established conclusion remains that the object of cognition is dependent upon the means of cognition;

for the proponents of Consciousness-Only (Vijñānavādins), having accepted the primacy of the means of cognition in the apprehension of an entity due to the rule of simultaneous perception, [this conclusion follows].
Having eliminated the external collection of measurable objects,

[the category] was reduced to being a mere name by the followers of Kaṇāda and Gautama, who established the determination of objects based on the adherence to [their own] definitions; for, according to the logic that "an object is apprehended through both sight and touch," when a single stable object of cognition exists, there are many [perceptions].

The theory of the convergence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇasaṃplava*)— namely, that there is a coalescence of means of valid cognition and the apprehension of many objects by a single means of valid cognition— is now introduced. This convergence applies without distinction to both the means of valid cognition and the object of cognition, being unrestricted in its application.

And he acts [thus]. However, the Buddhists have attributed here the position of "confusion" (*viplava*); accordingly, their twofoldness of objects—consisting of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—results in a twofoldness of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).
As it is stated in the *Pramāṇavārttika*: "The means of valid cognition is twofold because of the twofoldness of its objects."
(2/1) "The refutation of the number three [of categories] is due to the observation of only two objects of cognition" (2/64), and so forth.

Regarding the object that is a real entity (*vastu*), there is a disagreement between the Buddhists and others concerning whether it consists of the universal (*sāmānya*), the particular (*viśeṣa*), or the form of both combined.
In the systems of Kaṇāda and Gautama, it is not [viewed as] threefold by way of the division into the universal, the particular, and the possessor of those (*tadvat*).

Regarding the duality of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and objects of valid cognition (*prameya*), nor is there any confusion among the means of valid cognition regarding their respective objects;
as stated in Uddyotakara’s *Vārttika*: "First of all, there are not two means of valid cognition."
We proceed [in this way],
neither with two distinct objects nor with a confusion between them.

In the Buddhist view, however, it is accepted that there is a twofold nature of reality consisting of the universal and the particular, which are unmixed in form and characterized respectively by causal efficiency and its opposite; and on account of this, the duality of objects of cognition (*prameya*) is established.
In reality, however, even within the Buddhist system,
the substantiality of the universal (*sāmānya*) is merely superficially attractive;
for it is capable of imparting its form to the cognition, and it alone possesses causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*).
It has been stated that only the particular (*viśeṣa*) possesses the nature of a real entity (*vastutva*), and not the universal (*sāmānya*);

for it is said, "The object of cognition is thus only the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), because the accomplishment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) [occurs] through it. Even this being so, [cognition] is not entirely without an objective basis (*nirālambana*).
This is a conventional usage;
for it is precisely the particular that is perceived as a universal because it possesses a recurring form,
and it is that very particular which, by virtue of being the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the object of knowledge, is treated as common.
And because a universal must be admitted:
since it is the particular itself that serves as the locus for the exclusion of heterogeneous things,
therefore that very particular is [grasped] by a cognition of a recurring form as having a common nature.
It is not surprising that it should appear here;

for it has also been stated in the *Alaṅkārabhāṣya*: "When [a word] is perceived as being capable of directly producing cognition, then, because it is being characterized by its own form (*svarūpa*), [it is considered a denotation]."
The particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is that which is directly perceived;

however, when there is a cognition of that very same object through a causal chain because of its capacity [to produce it], then it is a characteristic in the form of a universal, and thus it is the "universal characteristic" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
By way of tradition, incapacity is simply capacity itself through the function of exclusion (paryudāsa-vṛtti),
and not the mere absence of capacity.

Since the specific particular (*viśeṣa*) alone is the true nature of a real entity by virtue of its being capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), it alone is also ultimately real (*paramārthasat*) because it is non-deceptive. This being the case, the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is unreal; for it appears only by depending upon the particular, and thus, appearing under another form and being accessible solely through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it is merely of a conventional nature.
By concealing that very [nature] while maintaining it through the power of existence, it becomes conventionally real (*saṃvṛtisat*).
Thus, because worldly transaction is indeed consistent even by means of that which is not ultimately real and is non-existent in the ultimate sense, [it is established].
Therefore, that which is like truth is indeed truth;

for this existence, appearing in the form of another, is just as dependent on entities as are those entities themselves, because it is constructed by conceptualization born from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of entities.
The existence of both being and non-being is established;
for although all three types of universals are equally non-existent, [they are nonetheless established].

Nevertheless, having understood the existence [of the probans] through the essential reason (svabhāvahetu) as having existence as its basis, through the non-apprehension reason (anupalabdhihetu) as having non-existence as its basis, and through the effect reason (kāryahetu) as having both as its basis;
Reality is indeed realized through all three types of means of knowledge;
however, the existence of things such as a double moon is not established even by other forms of evidence, such as their being objects of cognition.
Therefore, in no way whatsoever do those things which have become non-objects possess existence.
As it is stated in the *Pramāṇavārttika*: "Hair and so forth are not universals, because they are non-objects despite being adhered to as such."
And just as there is a determination of two distinct objects for a single existent by means of its own nature and the nature of others— that is, by means of its specific and general characteristics—
likewise, the single particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) alone is made the object of both perception and inference.

Therefore, worldly transaction proceeds precisely by unifying those two: that which is the perceived particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and that which is the conceptualized universal form (*sāmānyasvarūpa*).

The universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), although appearing as a real entity (*vastu*), becomes the object of a thing and the object of purposeful activity (*pravṛttiviṣaya*) when it is determined as a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
For this very reason, perception is connected with external reality.

The validity and reliability of inference are accepted on the grounds that it is connected to what is externally related. Intending all of this, Dharmottara stated: "Furthermore, an object that has been superimposed, when being apprehended, is determined as a particular (svalakṣaṇa), because..."

Consequently, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is established as the object of engagement for inference. Regarding this, Durveka stated: "Therefore, the object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) should not be described as being of two kinds; rather, only its single object of engagement should be made known. Thus, there is a distinction in the modes of apprehension of that very same [object].

Thus, this alone is the determinant of the distinction between the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and nothing else. And in this way, it follows that the object of cognition (prameya) called the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), which is the ultimate reality, is the sole object to be grasped by the means of valid cognition.
For that reality is indeed neither determinable nor expressible;
whereas that which is determined by the means of valid cognition is merely the other-nature, which is simply the universal.
And thus, even by way of both the ultimate and the conventional...
The establishment of the dyad of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and objects of valid cognition (*prameya*) is accepted by all Buddhists.
Thus, in the Sautrāntika system,

just as ultimate and conventional reality are accepted as the grounds for the existence of the object of cognition (*prameya*), they are likewise accepted as the grounds for the existence of the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The application [of the term] is not at all inconsistent;

for that which is called "specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*), the unique nature (*asādhāraṇa-svabhāva*) mentioned here, is, according to the Buddhist doctrine of realists (*vastuvādin*), nothing other than the atom (*paramāṇu*).

Furthermore, regarding the theory of atoms (*paramāṇuvāda*), although atoms are without distinction in that they are all indeed beyond the reach of the senses, they are differentiated within the Vaibhāṣika and Sautrāntika systems— which are not significantly distinct from one another— by the designations of "substantial atom" (*dravyaparamāṇu*), "aggregated atom" (*saṃghātaparamāṇu*), and "atom as a form of accumulation" (*saṃcitākāraparamāṇu*), in accordance with works such as the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Ālambanaparīkṣā*.

Nevertheless, because eight, nine, ten, eleven, and so forth arise simultaneously through the aggregation and accumulation of atoms (*aṇu*), the possession of tangibility (*sparśavattva*) is established among them. This is stated by accepting the doctrine of one's own school— that the possession of tangibility is pervaded by atomhood— or even without accepting it, [it is established] within the very atoms when they are conjoined, according to the theory of the whole (*avayavivāda*) as agreed upon by the followers of Kaṇāda and Gautama.
The perception of grossness and so forth is accepted. Since the existence of past and future time has been rejected among those who assert the three kinds of impermanent atoms mentioned above,
the Sautrāntika alone bears the title of "preeminent" (pradhāna).
By means of the doctrine of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*) and the doctrine of the continuum of moments (*kṣaṇasantativāda*) propounded by him, the most subtle form of a thing—

the nature of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is a conceptual reality (*prajñaptisat*) and a form belonging to a continuum— comes to be revealed. Furthermore, this substantial atom (*dravyaparamāṇu*) accepted by the Sautrāntikas is impermanent and all-pervasive.
This atom-moment (kṣaṇaparamāṇu), which is complete as being independent and distinct in terms of space, time, and intrinsic nature,
is perceived in the form of a continuum, an aggregate, and so forth.
In this [system], spatial, temporal, karmic, and causal results and so forth appear as fully developed through their relations and their intensification;
it is precisely by accepting such an atomic theory that [the proponents] are called realists (vastuvādins).
The Buddhists are distinguished from the non-Buddhist outsiders who assert the existence of external objects;
and this manner of distinction results in being identical regarding both the object of cognition (*prameya*) and the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
In the Vaiśeṣika system, the atom is eternal;
it is stable and serves as the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of the composite whole (avayavin) that is produced through the sequence beginning with the dyad (dvyaṇuka).
It is the substratum of qualities, actions, particularities, and so forth. However, the atom (paramāṇu) as conceived by the Buddhists,
though beyond the reach of the senses, is subject to momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) because it exists only for the duration of the present moment.
Therefore, it is impermanent;

it is established as being without parts and not the substratum of qualities, actions, and so forth. And thus, by accepting the atoms (paramāṇu) favored by the Buddhists, that which was asserted by Gautama and Kaṇāda—

The following doctrines have been refuted: that there exists a composite substance (*avayavidravya*) as the substratum of color and so forth, which is distinct from color and the rest and serves as the cause of a single cognition; that action (*karman*) is distinct from the successive moments of the hand and other limbs arising in different locations; and that the universal (*sāmānya*) is distinct from the individual (*vyakti*).

Therefore, all cognitions of substance, quality, action, and so forth, as maintained by the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas, are according to the Buddhist view based upon internal causes characterized by beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*);
they are mere designations (*prajñaptimātra*), and not dependent upon external objects. Thus...

Although this doctrine of eternal atoms was inherited from the Vaiśeṣika tradition, it was nevertheless refuted by earlier Buddhists by subjecting it to the consequence of momentary destruction; furthermore,
later thinkers established these inert atoms within the sphere of consciousness, thereby rendering them appearances of sentience.

The self-nature of this atom, which has become manifest as consciousness, is self-cognized; for the sake of the Neo-Buddhists who do not accept external objects, it reveals the non-dual nature of knowledge as being untainted and free from insentience.

Thus, having removed the gateway of the means of knowledge— which, according to the Buddhists' conception of atoms as having the nature of appearances, seems as if rendered inert by external, insentient non-appearances— the path of clear comprehension, which is accompanied by appearance and devoid of externality, is established for the determination of the status of valid cognition.
He descended. And this discussion will be clarified in its proper place.

Furthermore, by virtue of whether cognitions are formless (*nirākāra*) or possess form (*sākāra*), the existence of the real object that serves as their objective support (*ālambana*) is made manifest.
And the nature of knowledge, its validity, and the manner of its apprehension become known.

All Buddhist and non-Buddhist philosophers who maintain the theory of external objects (bāhyārthavādins)— namely the Vaiśeṣikas, Vaibhāṣikas, Sautrāntikas, and followers of Gautama— are proponents of the view that cognition is devoid of form (jñānanirākāravādins).
In their view, the existence of an object is revealed precisely by virtue of the fact that cognitions are formless.
And it is understood that this is the cause for awakening to the true nature of knowledge.

Furthermore, it has been stated that all philosophical systems, whether Buddhist or non-Buddhist, which maintain the reality of external objects, are proponents of the theory that knowledge is formless (*nirākāra*).
According to their view, this form which appears within knowledge—
It refers precisely to an object that is apprehended— whether stable or momentary— and which is distinct from the apprehending cognition.
For this very reason, in the case of perception, non-Buddhist Naiyāyikas [assert] it to be from a cognition devoid of form (*nirākāra-jñāna*).
In order to make known an object that is remote from it, there must be contact between the sense faculty and the object;
and the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas maintain that this is the "triple-contact" (trikasparśa) of the object, the faculty, and consciousness.

Although all Sarvāstivāda Buddhists are alike in asserting that cognition arises from a triad of contacts, there exists a distinction among them based on their respective theories of the apprehension of objects and the conformity of cognition to the object, as well as their views on whether these occur across three moments of time or at a single moment. Consequently, from the definition of perception provided by Vasubandhu— namely, "perception is that which is born from an object"— it is made known that there is an apprehension of an object that already exists prior [to the cognition].

The Sautrāntika position is accepted that there is a "representation" (*sārūpya*) of an atom— which exists for only a single moment— and of consciousness; thus, [this applies] to the triad of sense-faculty, object, and attention,
as well as to contact.

In the case of a distinct entity, its stability and momentariness alone are the determining factors. For a cognition, the very form appearing within it constitutes the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of the entity;
and this alone is the existence (*sattva*) of the entity.
By the very attainment of this [object], the correspondence of the cognition is established; and from that correspondence, its validity is accepted.
And thus, for both perception and inference, [validity is] directly—

Alternatively, validity is established through non-contradiction by means of the apprehension of the object, whether directly or through a succession [of cognitions], without distinction. Although even non-Buddhist Naiyāyikas maintain that the distinction [of cognitions] is due to the object itself because cognition is formless (*nirākāra*),
they do not admit the existence of the object (*vastu*) as being characterized by causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*).
By them, the position that cognition, the object, and the sense organ exist simultaneously at a single moment is rejected;
for this very reason, in their view, there is a temporal gap between the preceding moment and the present sense organ and object.

The production of the quality of cognition (jñāna-guṇa) belonging to the two parts of a whole (avayavin), which endure for three moments by virtue of their conjunction, is established as a tenet of our system.

Even though the followers of Kaṇāda and Gautama maintain that cognition is formless (*nirākāra*), because this does not contradict their doctrine of momentary existence, substances, qualities, and actions are understood as being both general and particular by virtue of possessing the nature of the higher and the lower universals (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*).
Furthermore, in that system, the convergence (*saṃplava*) of multiple means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not contradictory.
In the Buddhist view, however, the real entity is merely the particular (*viśeṣa*); the means of apprehending it is exclusively perception (*pratyakṣa*);
and everything distinct from that is merely a conceptual universal (*sāmānyamātra*), being purely adventitious.

Accepting the position that the apprehender of that [object] is inference (*anumāna*)—that is, the subsequent conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—and having established the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the object of valid cognition (*prameya*) as unmixed, the means of valid cognition postulated by others are subsumed within these two alone. This method of subsuming other means of valid cognition within [these two] belongs to the Buddhists; it was not devised by those more recent than them.

Almost all the authors of the Nyāya system who follow the Vedas have been compelled, whether by choice or against their will, to necessarily establish [the existence of God]; furthermore, they have subsumed other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) within inference (*anumāna*). Thus, according to the Buddhist view, although the collection of means of valid cognition—namely comparison (*upamāna*), verbal testimony (*śabda*), presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), and non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*)—is equal in being proponents of the theory that cognition is formless (*jñānanirākāravāda*), [they are nonetheless distinct].
In the Buddhist view, due to the absence of external forms (*nirākāratva*), cognition is non-conceptual with respect to its own part,
it apprehends only the ultimate reality,
and cognition is self-luminous (*svaprakāśatva*).
Furthermore, the doctrines concerning the intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) of the means of knowledge have been presented here along with their relevant implications;
however, in the Śāṅkara school, Brahman— which is the ultimate reality— is held to be within the scope of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Indeed, by treating as if it were his own position the Buddhist view that [perception] is non-conceptual, formless, self-luminous, and intrinsically valid, he cuts off his own concealment and severs his adherence to the Buddhist theory of valid cognition.

What need is there for much? The definitions of substance, quality, and action as conceived by the Nyāya school, as well as the refutation of the intrinsic nature of the whole (avayavin), universals (sāmānya), inherence (samavāya), conjunction (saṃyoga), and so forth, have already been performed by the earlier Sautrāntikas and others; this has been extensively reproduced in various ways through our own terminology in the Brahma-sūtras, Śaṅkara’s commentary (bhāṣya), its sub-commentaries (ṭīkā), and other works.
And it has been established.
What more need be said? Based upon either two truths or three truths, the non-dualist doctrine (advaitavāda) rooted in the theory of falsity was [established] by the venerable Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda.

For that which has been explained is merely an imitation of the Sautrāntikas' doctrine of the dual existence of things, consisting of both the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the universal (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). It is not hidden that in the Buddhist view, based precisely upon the particular, the false universal is determined as a real entity.
In the same way, within the doctrine of Brahman, multiplicity— which has Brahman as its substratum—
appears even though it is false;
this is because the particular (svalakṣaṇa) is distinct from cognition and is infinite in number.
Indeed, even that apparent difference which is perceived due to Brahman’s nature as consciousness and its unity is refuted in the Vijñānavāda school.
It arises as if [so]. Indeed, this is omitted here for fear of prolixity.

There is yet another point worthy of attention regarding the excellence of the Buddhist investigation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): generally, the systematic establishment of the means of valid cognition by all proponents—both Buddhist and non-Buddhist, realist and anti-realist—is for the very purpose of establishing external objects.
It was brought to full development by that very same Nāgārjuna, Āryadeva, and others;

and thus the unshakable conventional discourse of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and objects of cognition (*prameya*), which is accepted by the Sarvāstivādins, [was established] upon the diamond-thunderbolt of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
It was shaken and shattered;

and following that, even the Śaṅkara-advaitins, such as Śrī Harṣa, Citsukha, and others, have haughtily brought the substantialist doctrines of the Sāṃkhya, Ulūka, and others to their complete end. This being so—
In the stream of philosophical systems, the position of the Buddhist logicians is most remarkable,
in that Dignāga, Dharmakīrti, and others— while negating the existence of external objects such as the knower and the known apart from consciousness— [nevertheless...]

By virtue of the doctrine of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), the Indian science of epistemology (*pramāṇaśāstra*) has been rendered unassailable and brought to the highest pinnacle of logical excellence.
Following this novel approach, the Vedists and the proponents of non-dualism (*advaitavādins*)...
The treatises on valid cognition (*pramāṇa-śāstra*) were not practiced in accordance with their respective systems;
however, certain recent texts that have been found—
These [views] are for the most part rooted in the imitation of the systems of Gautama, Bhaṭṭa, Prabhākara, and others.
Initially, there was an established system for the proof of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) based solely on the objects of cognition (*prameya*);
and it was in accordance with that very [system] that Dharmakīrti also [formulated his views] in his own *Pramāṇavārttika*.

It is a traditional view among Buddhist scholars that the Sautrāntika school predominantly accepts the doctrine of real existence (*vastusadvāda*). A thorough understanding of this system can only be achieved by examining numerous commentaries translated into the Tibetan language.

This must be determined. In reality, however, it is understood—both from the *Pramāṇavārttika* and from an examination of Manorathanandin’s commentary and the *Alaṅkārabhāṣya*—that this work, devoted to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is compatible with all three views: external existence, non-existence, and both. For those who maintain the existence of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*), the causal relationship [is established] even without an external object.
The relationship between the known and the knower, as well as the conventional practice of inference, is not accepted in the absence of that [external object];
however, Dignāga, Dharmakīrti, and others understand the Vijñānavāda to be neither contradictory nor unfavorable for the discernment of the nature of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*).
It is not so for the doctrine of external objects (*bāhyārthavāda*).

Even though, in the context of establishing the validity of cognition (*jñānaprāmāṇya*) by depending solely on the existence of an external object as the object of knowledge (*prameya*), [validity] consists in the capacity for purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*), [it is not so for us].
The attainment of the object, the determination of the object,
and in the case of perception, the cognition arising from the sense organs and so forth.
At first glance, it appears that in inference there is a relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*),
and that from smoke the cognition of fire arises, and so forth; nevertheless, all of this—
For worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is employed in the world precisely on the basis of appearance,
and it is also investigated in the treatises (*śāstra*),
even in the position that accepts external objects.

And because the external object is also apprehended solely through the power of its appearance (*pratibhāsa*), the Vijñānavādins undertake an investigation into the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that is identical in form for both the theories of the external and the internal.
Those who maintain the existence of external objects accept that the cause for the cognition of a determinate form is the external object itself;
however, whether it be an external [object]...

Whether it be a specific awakened latent impression (*vāsanā*) or the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) that acts as the regulator by way of awakening [the cognition], there is still no contradiction with worldly practice (*vyavahāra*).
The investigation into external objects undertaken by the Vijñānavādins and Naiyāyikas is not conducted with regard to external objects themselves.
Moreover, cognition becomes a penetrator of reality through its dependence upon the exchange [of mental impressions].

As it is stated in the *Pramāṇavārttika*: "Having disregarded the true nature of those [objects], the investigation of external things is extended. For some person, something specific within serves as the activator of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).

And thus: "Therefore, there is an exchange of cognitions, not a dependence on external objects. Furthermore, by the Vijñānavādins, who uphold the doctrine that "the very apprehension [of an object] is its existence," no purpose is admitted to be served by an external object, but rather by the manifestation itself.
For it is well known that a manifestation occurs even without an external object.
This being so, in the inference of fire from smoke, there is the cognition consisting of the manifestation of smoke.

Being bound by the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of fire, it produces a cognition appearing as fire through the power of the causal complex of a single cognition. In reality, however, according to the system of the master Dharmakīrti, the latent impression alone is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) by virtue of its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*); and that [impression] is of the nature of a mental appearance (*pratibhāsa*).
For that which is the object of cognition from the perspective of ultimate reality— even in the theory of external objects— is not inferred as an external fire existing at that very moment,
because at a single time there can be no thorough knowledge of both cause and effect; rather, [it is inferred] as follows:
It is both future and past; and fire, being both future and past, is indeed of the nature of a manifestation.
For this very reason, it is not [perceived] by that which is non-manifesting.
In the discussion regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), some purpose is established by means of fire.
Likewise, it is latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) alone that constitutes the future manifestation; and being perceived as a unity, it becomes the motivator of action.
And it is said in the *Pramāṇavārttika*: "In that case as well, a cognition appearing as smoke, by virtue of its potent latent impression (*vāsanā*),
would lead only to a cognition appearing as fire, not to the fire itself."
However, that which follows the Sautrāntika doctrine— the establishment of two types of entities by way of their specific and general forms in relation to external objects,
and the corresponding twofold nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)— was set forth by Dignāga, Dharmakīrti, and others.
That which has been established is indeed entirely consistent, because of the observed necessity of simultaneous apprehension.
For that doctrine of dual form (dvairūpya) which was formulated by the Teacher (Ācārya) with reference to external objects was established solely from the perspective of others.
This is not with respect to the Vijñānavāda;
rather, out of deference to learned members of our own school, when it comes to the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the Vijñānavāda itself is the refuge.
In either case, the established doctrine of the dual nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*) is consistent.
And it has been stated by the Teacher:
There is indeed a doctrine among the learned that [the two-fold nature] is described by relying on external objects;
and that [nature] is established through the rule of simultaneous cognition.
